title: A 7am-1pm port call is not a day ashore.
subtitle: The two columns of times decide your holiday. The port names barely matter.

text: Nobody reads the two columns that matter.
sub: Every itinerary prints an arrival and a departure beside each port. Those numbers are the whole design of the week, and they are set in ship's time.

title: What each shape of day actually gives you

points.value: A real day. Breakfast ashore, lunch inland, back aboard without hurrying.
Half a day, and an hour of it is the queue for a boat.
You arrive as the town shuts for the afternoon and leave before it reopens.
Six hours, minus all-aboard at 15:30. Call it four and a half.

points.label: Overnight in port
points.value: Dinner ashore and an empty morning street. The best line in any itinerary.

items.head: All-aboard, not departure
items.body: Published 30 to 60 minutes before the ship sails, and stated in ship's time - which need not match your phone.

items.head: The tender queue, both ways
items.body: At an anchorage the last tender back is a separate, earlier time. Budget an hour of the day to boats.

items.head: The coach to the actual place
items.body: Some ports sit two hours from the thing you came for. That is four of your six hours, on a motorway.

text: Judge a sailing by its clock, not its map.
sub: Add up the hours genuinely ashore once all-aboard and the tenders are deducted. On most glossy itineraries the honest total is half of what the brochure implies.

title: Send me an itinerary and I'll read the clock.
body: Two lines back: what those arrival times really give you, and which day is the one you'd have regretted. No charge and no pitch.
